nodes.summary: For a predicate $p$ on keys and a tree $t$ with cached heights, $\mathrm{All}(p, t)$ holds if and only if $p(x)$ holds for every $x \in t$, where $x \in t$ means that $x$ is the key of some node of $t$.
nodes.title: The all-keys predicate in terms of membership (AVL trees)

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys from a linearly ordered type and a cached height at each node, and suppose $t$ is ordered: at every node, all keys in the left subtree are strictly smaller and all keys in the right subtree are strictly larger than the key at that node. Let $m$ be the leftmost key of $t$, or an arbitrary default value if $t$ is empty. Then every key of the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its…
nodes.title: Keys left after removing the minimum exceed it

nodes.summary: For a predicate $p$ on keys and a tree $t$ with cached heights, $\mathrm{All}(p, t)$ holds if and only if $p$ holds at every key of the plain binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing its cached heights. This holds by definition.
nodes.title: The all-keys predicate is unchanged by erasing height caches

nodes.summary: For a predicate $p$ on keys and a tree $t$ with cached heights, $\mathrm{All}(p, t)$ holds when $p$ holds at the key of every node of $t$. It is defined as the corresponding predicate on the plain binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing its cached heights.
nodes.title: Every key of an AVL tree satisfies a predicate

nodes.summary: Let $l$ and $r$ be trees with cached heights, let $x$ be a key, and write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree). If $h(l) \le h(r) + 1$ and $h(r) \le h(l) + 1$, then $\mathrm{balance}(l, x, r)$ is the node with left subtree $l$, key $x$, right subtree $r$ and cached height $\max(h(l), h(r)) + 1$; no rotation is performed.
nodes.title: Rebalancing when the heights of the children differ by at most one

nodes.summary: Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree), $\langle c; A, y, B \rangle$ for the node with cached height $c$, left subtree $A$, key $y$ and right subtree $B$, and $N(A, y, B)$ for the node $\langle \max(h(A), h(B)) + 1; A, y, B \rangle$. Let $A$, $B$, $C$, $R$ be trees with cached heights, let $x$, $y$, $z$ be keys and let $c$, $c'$ be natural numbers. If $h(R) + 1 < c$…
nodes.title: Left-right double rotation in AVL rebalancing

nodes.summary: Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree), $\langle c; A, y, B \rangle$ for the node with cached height $c$, left subtree $A$, key $y$ and right subtree $B$, and $N(A, y, B)$ for the node $\langle \max(h(A), h(B)) + 1; A, y, B \rangle$. Let $A$, $B$, $R$ be trees with cached heights, let $x$, $y$ be keys and let $c$ be a natural number. If $h(R) + 1 < c$ and…
nodes.title: Single right rotation in AVL rebalancing

nodes.summary: Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree), $\langle c; A, y, B \rangle$ for the node with cached height $c$, left subtree $A$, key $y$ and right subtree $B$, and $N(A, y, B)$ for the node $\langle \max(h(A), h(B)) + 1; A, y, B \rangle$. Let $L$, $A$, $B$, $C$ be trees with cached heights, let $x$, $y$, $z$ be keys and let $c$, $c'$ be natural numbers. If $h(L) + 1 < c$…
nodes.title: Right-left double rotation in AVL rebalancing

nodes.summary: Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree), $\langle c; A, y, B \rangle$ for the node with cached height $c$, left subtree $A$, key $y$ and right subtree $B$, and $N(A, y, B)$ for the node $\langle \max(h(A), h(B)) + 1; A, y, B \rangle$. Let $L$, $A$, $B$ be trees with cached heights, let $x$, $y$ be keys and let $c$ be a natural number. If $h(L) + 1 < c$ and…
nodes.title: Single left rotation in AVL rebalancing

nodes.summary: For trees $l$, $r$ with cached heights and a key $x$, write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree) and $N(A, y, B)$ for the node with left subtree $A$, key $y$, right subtree $B$ and cached height $\max(h(A), h(B)) + 1$. The node $\mathrm{balance}(l, x, r)$ is defined by cases. If $h(l) > h(r) + 1$ and $l$ has left subtree $A$, key $y$ and right subtree $B$, it is the…
nodes.title: AVL rebalancing

nodes.summary: Let $l$ and $r$ be trees whose cached heights are correct at every node and which are balanced (at every node the cached heights of the two subtrees differ by at most one), let $x$ be a key, and write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$ (zero for the empty tree). If $h(l) \le h(r) + 2$ and $h(r) \le h(l) + 2$, then $\mathrm{balance}(l, x, r)$ is balanced.
nodes.title: AVL rebalancing yields a balanced tree

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with a cached height at each node whose cached heights are correct, and which is balanced: at every node the cached heights of the two subtrees differ by at most one. Then the tree obtained from $t$ by minimum deletion (removing its leftmost key, rebalancing on the way back up) is again balanced.
nodes.title: Minimum deletion preserves AVL balance

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys from a linearly ordered type and a cached height at each node, whose cached heights are correct, and which is balanced: at every node the cached heights of the two subtrees differ by at most one. Then for every key $x$, the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$, rebalancing along the search path, is again balanced.
nodes.title: Deleting a key preserves AVL balance

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with a cached height at each node whose cached heights are correct, and which is balanced: at every node the cached heights of the two subtrees differ by at most one. Then the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its leftmost key, rebalancing on the way back up, is again balanced.
nodes.title: Removing the minimum preserves AVL balance

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys from a linearly ordered type and a cached height at each node, whose cached heights are correct, and which is balanced: at every node the cached heights of the two subtrees differ by at most one. Then for every key $x$, the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$, rebalancing along the search path, is again balanced.
nodes.title: Deletion preserves AVL balance

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ over a linearly ordered type, the AVL tree built from $L$ by successive insertion satisfies the AVL balance invariant.
nodes.title: AVL trees built from a list are balanced

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, let $t$ be an AVL tree over $\alpha$ and let $x \in \alpha$. If $t$ has correct cached heights and satisfies the AVL balance invariant, then the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ also satisfies the AVL balance invariant.
nodes.title: AVL insertion preserves balance

nodes.summary: Let $\ell$ and $r$ be AVL trees that satisfy the AVL balance invariant, and write $h(\ell)$ and $h(r)$ for the heights cached at their roots (with height $0$ for the empty tree). If $h(\ell) \le h(r) + 1$ and $h(r) \le h(\ell) + 1$, then for every key $k$ the node built from $\ell$, $k$ and $r$ by the smart constructor, which stores the height $\max(h(\ell), h(r)) + 1$, satisfies the AVL balance invariant.
nodes.title: The AVL node constructor preserves balance

nodes.summary: The empty tree is balanced. A node with left subtree $\ell$ and right subtree $r$ is balanced when $\ell$ and $r$ are balanced and $h(\ell) \le h(r) + 1$ and $h(r) \le h(\ell) + 1$, where $h$ denotes the height cached at the root of a tree (and $0$ for the empty tree). Equivalently, at every node the balance factor $h(\ell) - h(r)$ lies in $\{-1, 0, 1\}$.
nodes.title: AVL balance invariant

nodes.summary: If two AVL trees $\ell$ and $r$ have correct cached heights, then for every key $k$ the tree produced by the rebalancing function from $\ell$, $k$ and $r$ also has correct cached heights.
nodes.title: AVL rebalancing preserves cached heights

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with a cached height at each node whose cached heights are correct: each node stores one more than the larger of the cached heights of its two subtrees, the empty tree having height $0$. Then the cached heights of the tree obtained from $t$ by minimum deletion (removing its leftmost key, rebalancing on the way back up) are again correct.
nodes.title: Minimum deletion keeps cached heights correct

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys from a linearly ordered type and a cached height at each node whose cached heights are correct: each node stores one more than the larger of the cached heights of its two subtrees, the empty tree having height $0$. Then for every key $x$, the cached heights of the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$, rebalancing along the search path, are again correct.
nodes.title: Deleting a key keeps cached heights correct

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with a cached height at each node whose cached heights are correct: each node stores one more than the larger of the cached heights of its two subtrees, the empty tree having height $0$. Then the cached heights of the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its leftmost key, rebalancing on the way back up, are again correct.
nodes.title: Removing the minimum keeps cached heights correct

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a binary tree with keys from a linearly ordered type and a cached height at each node whose cached heights are correct: each node stores one more than the larger of the cached heights of its two subtrees, the empty tree having height $0$. Then for every key $x$, the cached heights of the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$, rebalancing along the search path, are again correct.
nodes.title: Deletion keeps cached heights correct

nodes.summary: For every list $L$ over a linearly ordered type, the AVL tree built from $L$ by successive insertion has correct cached heights.
nodes.title: AVL trees built from a list have correct cached heights

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. If an AVL tree $t$ over $\alpha$ has correct cached heights, then for every $x \in \alpha$ the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ also has correct cached heights.
nodes.title: AVL insertion preserves cached heights

nodes.summary: If two AVL trees $\ell$ and $r$ have correct cached heights, then for every key $k$ the node built from $\ell$, $k$ and $r$ by the smart constructor, which stores the height $\max(h(\ell), h(r)) + 1$ where $h$ denotes the height cached at the root (and $0$ for the empty tree), also has correct cached heights.
nodes.title: The AVL node constructor preserves cached heights

nodes.summary: The empty tree has correct cached heights. A node storing the height $c$, with left subtree $\ell$ and right subtree $r$, has correct cached heights when $\ell$ and $r$ have correct cached heights and $c = \max(h(\ell), h(r)) + 1$, where $h$ denotes the height cached at the root of a tree (and $0$ for the empty tree).
nodes.title: Correct cached heights

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and let $t$ be an ordered AVL tree over $\alpha$. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, searching for $x$ in $t$ by following comparisons from the root returns true if and only if $x$ is a key of $t$.
nodes.title: Correctness of AVL search

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$ and a key $x$, the search for $x$ returns false on the empty tree; at a node with key $k$ it searches the left subtree if $x < k$, searches the right subtree if $k < x$, and returns true otherwise. The cached heights are ignored.
nodes.title: Membership search in an AVL tree

nodes.summary: Minimum deletion maps a binary tree with cached heights to the tree obtained by removing its leftmost key and rebalancing on the way back up. It is the operation of removing the minimum, under the name used for the successor step of deletion, where a deleted node with two children is replaced by the minimum of its right subtree.
nodes.title: Minimum deletion in an AVL tree

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, a key $x \in \alpha$ and a tree $t$ with cached heights, $\mathrm{delete}(x, t)$ is defined to be $\mathrm{erase}(x, t)$, the AVL deletion of $x$ from $t$.
nodes.title: AVL tree deletion under its alternative name

nodes.summary: For a tree $t$ with cached heights, the tree obtained by removing the leftmost key of $t$ is defined by recursion on $t$. The empty tree stays empty. A node whose left subtree is empty is replaced by its right subtree. A node with nonempty left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$ is replaced by $\mathrm{balance}(l', k, r)$, where $l'$ is $l$ with its leftmost key removed and $\mathrm{balance}$ is the AVL…
nodes.title: Removing the leftmost key of an AVL tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $x \in \alpha$. Deleting $x$ from a tree with cached heights is defined by recursion on the tree, where $\mathrm{balance}$ denotes the AVL rebalancing function. The empty tree stays empty. For a node with left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$: if $x < k$, the result is $\mathrm{balance}(l', k, r)$, where $l'$ is $l$ with $x$ deleted; if $k < x$, the result is…
nodes.title: AVL tree deletion

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, the tree built from the empty list is the empty tree, and the tree built from a list with head $x$ and tail $xs$ is obtained by AVL insertion of $x$ into the tree built from $xs$. Thus the list is inserted from right to left, starting from the empty tree.
nodes.title: Building an AVL tree from a list

nodes.summary: Let $l$ and $r$ be trees whose cached heights are correct at every node, and write $h$ for the cached height. Then for every key $k$, the rebalanced node $b$ built from $l$, $k$ and $r$ satisfies $h(b) \le \max(h(l), h(r)) + 1$.
nodes.title: Upper bound on height after AVL rebalancing

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$, and $t$ a tree whose cached heights are correct. Then the cached height of the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ is at most the cached height of $t$.
nodes.title: Deletion does not increase the height of an AVL tree

nodes.summary: If $t$ is a tree whose cached heights are correct, then the cached height of the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its leftmost key is at most the cached height of $t$.
nodes.title: Removing the leftmost key does not increase the height of an AVL tree

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, if a tree $t$ has correct cached heights at every node, then for every key $x$ the cached height of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is at most the cached height of $t$ plus one.
nodes.title: Upper bound on height after AVL insertion

nodes.summary: The cached height of the empty tree is $0$, and the cached height of a node is the height value stored at that node, so it is read off the root in constant time.
nodes.title: Cached height of an AVL tree

nodes.summary: Given a tree $t$ and a list $s$, this is the list of keys of $t$ in inorder (left subtree, root key, right subtree, recursively) followed by $s$. It is computed in linear time by the binary search tree traversal of $t$ with its cached heights erased.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal of an AVL tree onto a suffix

nodes.summary: For all trees $l$ and $r$ and every key $k$, the inorder traversal of the rebalanced node built from $l$, $k$ and $r$ is the inorder traversal of $l$, followed by $k$, followed by the inorder traversal of $r$.
nodes.title: AVL rebalancing preserves the inorder traversal

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$, and $t$ an ordered tree. Then the inorder traversal of $\mathrm{delete}(x, t)$, the AVL deletion of $x$ from $t$ under its alternative name, is the inorder traversal of $t$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed; if $x$ does not occur, the traversal is unchanged.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal after AVL deletion, alternative name

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a nonempty tree with cached heights and $m$ its leftmost key. Then the inorder traversal of $t$ is $m$ followed by the inorder traversal of the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its leftmost key.
nodes.title: The inorder traversal begins with the leftmost key

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$, and $t$ an ordered tree. Then the inorder traversal of the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ is the inorder traversal of $t$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed; if $x$ does not occur, the traversal is unchanged.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal after AVL deletion

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered type $\alpha$, if an AVL tree is ordered, then its inorder traversal contains no key twice.
nodes.title: The inorder traversal of an ordered AVL tree has no duplicates

nodes.summary: For every AVL tree $t$, the inorder traversal of $t$ equals the binary search tree inorder traversal of the binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing its cached heights; this holds by definition.
nodes.title: AVL inorder traversal agrees with the erased binary search tree

nodes.summary: The inorder traversal of a tree $t$ lists its keys with the left subtree first, then the root key, then the right subtree, recursively. It is the binary search tree inorder traversal of $t$ with its cached heights erased, computed in linear time.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal of an AVL tree

nodes.summary: Let the keys be linearly ordered, and write $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$ for the AVL rebalancing of the node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$. Inserting $x$ into the empty tree gives the node with key $x$, two empty children and cached height $1$. Inserting $x$ into a node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$ gives $\mathrm{balance}(L', k, R)$, where $L'$ is the result of…
nodes.title: Insertion into an AVL tree

nodes.summary: Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$, with $h$ of the empty tree equal to $0$, and write $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$ for the AVL rebalancing of the node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$. If $L$ and $R$ are trees whose cached heights are correct at every node, then for every key $k$ we have $\max(h(L), h(R)) \le h(\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R))$.
nodes.title: Rebalancing does not drop below the taller child

nodes.summary: If $t$ is a tree whose cached heights are correct and which is balanced, then the cached height of $t$ is at most one more than the cached height of the tree obtained from $t$ by removing its leftmost key.
nodes.title: Removing the leftmost key lowers the height of an AVL tree by at most one

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$, and $t$ a balanced tree whose cached heights are correct. Then the cached height of $t$ is at most one more than the cached height of the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$.
nodes.title: Deletion lowers the height of an AVL tree by at most one

nodes.summary: Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$, with $h$ of the empty tree equal to $0$. Let the keys be linearly ordered, and let $T$ be a tree whose cached heights are correct at every node and which satisfies the AVL balance invariant at every node. Then for every key $x$, if $T'$ is the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$, we have $h(T) \le h(T')$.
nodes.title: Insertion does not lower the height

nodes.summary: Write $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$ for the AVL rebalancing of the node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$. For trees $L$ and $R$ and keys $k$ and $x$, the key $x$ lies in $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$ if and only if $x$ lies in $L$, $x = k$, or $x$ lies in $R$.
nodes.title: Membership after AVL rebalancing

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights whose keys come from a linearly ordered type, and let $x$ and $y$ be keys with $y \ne x$. If $y$ occurs in $T$, then $y$ occurs in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$. No search-tree ordering of $T$ is assumed.
nodes.title: AVL deletion keeps every other key

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights over a linearly ordered type, ordered as a search tree (every key in a left subtree is smaller, and every key in a right subtree is larger, than the key at the node). Then for all keys $x$ and $y$, $y$ occurs in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$ if and only if $y$ occurs in $T$ and $y \ne x$.
nodes.title: Keys of an ordered AVL tree after deletion

nodes.summary: Let the keys be linearly ordered. A key lies in the tree obtained by inserting the entries of a list one at a time, from last to first, into the empty tree exactly when it is in the list.
nodes.title: Membership in an AVL tree built from a list

nodes.summary: A key $x$ occurs in the inorder traversal of a tree $T$ if and only if $x$ lies in $T$.
nodes.title: Membership in the inorder traversal of an AVL tree

nodes.summary: Let the keys be linearly ordered. A key $y$ lies in the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into a tree $T$ if and only if $y = x$ or $y$ lies in $T$.
nodes.title: Membership after insertion into an AVL tree

nodes.summary: A key $x$ lies in a tree $T$ if and only if $x$ lies in the binary tree obtained from $T$ by erasing the cached heights.
nodes.title: AVL membership is membership in the underlying binary tree

nodes.summary: A key $x$ belongs to a tree $T$ when $x$ belongs to the binary tree obtained from $T$ by erasing the cached heights. Equivalently, no key belongs to the empty tree, and $x$ belongs to a node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$ exactly when $x$ belongs to $L$, $x = k$, or $x$ belongs to $R$.
nodes.title: Membership in an AVL tree

nodes.summary: For every nonempty binary tree $T$ with cached heights and every default value $d$, the leftmost key of $T$ computed with default $d$ occurs in $T$.
nodes.title: The leftmost key lies in the tree

nodes.summary: Given a default value $d$ and a binary tree $T$ with cached heights, the leftmost key of $T$ with default $d$ is $d$ when $T$ is empty; when $T$ has left subtree $L$ and root key $k$, it is the leftmost key of $L$ with default $k$. Thus for a nonempty tree it is the key of the node reached from the root by following left children as far as possible, and it does not depend on $d$.
nodes.title: Leftmost key of a tree

nodes.summary: Write $h(T)$ for the cached height at the root of a tree $T$, with $h$ of the empty tree equal to $0$. Given trees $L$ and $R$ and a key $k$, this is the node with left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$ whose cached height is $\max(h(L), h(R)) + 1$.
nodes.title: AVL node with computed height

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights over a linearly ordered type, ordered as a search tree. Then for every key $x$, $x$ does not occur in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$.
nodes.title: Deletion removes the deleted key from an ordered AVL tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, let $k \in \alpha$, and let $L$ and $R$ be ordered trees with cached heights over $\alpha$ such that every key of $L$ is less than $k$ and every key of $R$ is greater than $k$. Then the tree that rebalancing produces from left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$ is ordered.
nodes.title: Rebalancing an AVL node preserves the search-tree order

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights over a linearly ordered type. If $T$ is ordered as a search tree, then so is the tree obtained by the minimum-removal step used for the successor in deletion, which removes the leftmost key of $T$ and rebalances on the way back up.
nodes.title: Successor-step minimum removal preserves search-tree order

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights over a linearly ordered type. If $T$ is ordered as a search tree, then for every key $x$ the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$ with rebalancing is again ordered as a search tree.
nodes.title: Deleting a key from an ordered AVL tree keeps it ordered

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights over a linearly ordered type. If $T$ is ordered as a search tree, then so is the tree obtained from $T$ by removing its leftmost key and rebalancing on the way back up.
nodes.title: Removing the leftmost key preserves search-tree order

nodes.summary: Let $T$ be a binary tree with cached heights over a linearly ordered type, ordered as a search tree (every key in a left subtree is smaller, and every key in a right subtree is larger, than the key at the node). Then for every key $x$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$ with rebalancing is again ordered as a search tree.
nodes.title: AVL deletion preserves search-tree order

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For every list $xs$ of elements of $\alpha$, the tree obtained from the empty tree by inserting the elements of $xs$ one at a time, from the last element to the first, is ordered.
nodes.title: AVL trees built from a list are ordered

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. If a tree $t$ with cached heights over $\alpha$ is ordered, then in the inorder traversal of $t$ every key is less than every key that comes after it.
nodes.title: The inorder traversal of an ordered AVL tree is strictly increasing

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For every key $x \in \alpha$ and every ordered tree $t$ with cached heights over $\alpha$, the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is ordered.
nodes.title: AVL insertion preserves the search-tree order

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $<$. A tree $t$ with cached heights over $\alpha$ is ordered if and only if the binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing the cached heights is an ordered binary search tree.
nodes.title: Order of an AVL tree via its underlying binary tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $<$. A tree with cached heights over $\alpha$ is ordered when the binary tree obtained by erasing its cached heights is an ordered binary search tree: the empty tree is ordered, and a node with key $k$ is ordered when its left and right subtrees are ordered, every key of the left subtree is less than $k$, and every key of the right subtree is greater than $k$.
nodes.title: Ordered AVL trees

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type. Erasing the cached heights sends a tree with cached heights over $\alpha$ to a binary tree over $\alpha$: the empty tree goes to the empty binary tree, and a node with height $h$, left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$ goes to the binary-tree node with key $k$ whose left and right subtrees are the erasures of $L$ and $R$.
nodes.title: Erasing the cached heights of an AVL tree

nodes.summary: For a type $\alpha$, a tree with cached heights over $\alpha$ (the underlying type of AVL trees) is either empty, or a node made of a natural number $h$ (its cached height), a left subtree, a key in $\alpha$ and a right subtree.
nodes.title: Binary trees with cached heights
Computer Science

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
